beats.lead: Some beetles smell bad to survive. Bombardier beetles decided that was not dramatic enough.
beats.text: When threatened, a bombardier beetle mixes two chemicals stored in separate sacs inside its abdomen and fires the reaction straight at whatever is attacking it, with an audible pop.
beats.note: Natural History Museum beetle curator Max Barclay explains that a handful of related beetles use milder chemical defences, but bombardier beetles took the idea to an extreme.

beats.text: The chemicals are hydrogen peroxide and a hydroquinone, and mixing them is a genuinely violent reaction: the spray comes out scalding hot and under real pressure, fired in rapid pulses rather than one continuous stream.
beats.note: A tough chamber at the rear of the abdomen contains the reaction, so even an accidental discharge just fires harmlessly out the back rather than injuring the beetle itself.

beats.context: roughly how hot the beetle's defensive spray gets, hot enough that one species, the African bombardier beetle, can aim it in almost any direction, including back over its own body.

beats.lead: Charles Darwin found out about this the hard way, almost two centuries before the chemistry was explained.
beats.text: In an 1846 letter, Darwin described grabbing two ground beetles by hand and, rather than let a third species escape, popping one of the beetles into his mouth. It responded by firing its chemical defence down his throat.
beats.note: The beetle in that story was a close relative of true bombardier beetles rather than one itself, but a demonstration of the same basic strategy.

beats.text: The defence still works after a beetle has already been eaten. In one study, Japanese toads that swallowed bombardier beetles vomited 43% of them back up alive, mostly within 12 to 107 minutes, and more than 93% of those survivors were still alive at least two weeks later.

beats.line: Getting eaten is not necessarily the end of the story, if you can still detonate from the inside.
